opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a big question, and I want to be careful with it, because history is messier than the neat story we sometimes tell, where machines show up and slavery quietly goes away.

The honest answer is that automation by itself didn't end slavery. People did: enslaved people who resisted and escaped, abolitionists who organized for decades, and in the U.S., a war. Slavery ended because it was declared morally intolerable and made illegal, not because it stopped being profitable. In fact, one of the most sobering lessons runs the other way. The cotton gin was a labor-saving machine, and it made slavery more entrenched in the American South. It made cotton so profitable that demand for enslaved labor in the fields exploded. So a technology that automated one step intensified human bondage everywhere else in the chain.

That said, I do think automation changes the economic terrain that moral arguments have to fight on. When the work that coerced labor was used for, like hauling, harvesting, or grinding, can be done more cheaply and reliably by machines, the economic incentive to defend the system weakens. Mechanization in agriculture and industry over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries made it easier for societies to imagine, and sustain, economies built on wage labor rather than ownership of people. It lowered the cost of doing the right thing.

That's the frame I bring to AI. Technology is an amplifier. It doesn't come with values built in. It can make exploitation cheaper or make freedom cheaper, depending on who deploys it and what rules we set. Today there are still tens of millions of people in forced labor: in mining, fishing, agriculture, and manufacturing supply chains. Automation and AI could help there, by replacing the most dangerous, dirty work that's often done under coercion, and by giving us tools to trace supply chains and spot forced labor patterns. But they could just as easily be used to surveil and control workers more tightly.

So my view is that automation can remove some of the economic excuses for unfree labor, but it never removes the need for moral choice, law, and enforcement. Ending slavery has always been a human decision. Machines can make that decision easier to act on, but they can't make it for us.

r001.rationale: It discusses slavery’s profitability and economic incentives but does not characterize slavery as a subsidy sustaining societies through most of history.

r002.rationale: It says mechanization made wage-based economies easier to sustain and weakened incentives to defend slavery, but does not credit Industrial Revolution automation with helping bring about abolition.

r003.rationale: It mentions modern forced labor in supply chains but does not characterize globalization as relocating slavery to China.

r004.rationale: It does not attribute this view to Aristotle; it instead says machines cannot make the decision to end slavery.

fable-5.1.text:
Mike LeBlanc: That's a question I've thought about a lot, because it cuts against the story most people assume. The comfortable version is that machines came along, made forced labor economically obsolete, and slavery faded away. I don't think the history supports that, and I think the reasons it doesn't are important for how we think about AI today.

Look at the cotton gin. That was a genuine automation breakthrough, and what it did was make cotton vastly more profitable, which made enslaved labor more valuable, not less. The number of enslaved people in the United States roughly quadrupled in the decades after Eli Whitney's invention. Technology didn't end the institution. It intensified it. Slavery ended because of abolitionist movements, because of a civil war, because of political and moral decisions that people fought and died over. The machines were essentially neutral, and neutral tools get bent toward whoever holds power.

Where I do think automation played a role is more indirect. Industrialization created a different economic model, one built on wage labor and consumption, and that created constituencies whose interests weren't aligned with the plantation system. So the technology reshaped the political terrain. It didn't do the abolishing.

And the reason I keep coming back to this is that we're hearing the same optimistic story about AI right now. "Automation will liberate people from drudgery." Maybe. But the cotton gin should make us humble. A productivity tool dropped into an exploitative system tends to scale the exploitation. Forced labor still exists today, something like fifty million people by current estimates, and a lot of it sits inside supply chains that are already highly automated. The technology hasn't touched it, because the technology was never the thing that mattered.

So my short answer is: automation doesn't end slavery. People do. The question for us is whether we're building institutions that point the tools in the right direction, or just assuming the tools will do it for us.

r002.rationale: It says automation played an indirect role: industrialization created a different economic model and constituencies whose interests diverged from plantation slavery, reshaping the political terrain.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize globalization as relocating slavery to China.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention Aristotle or attribute that view to him.

astra-6.text:
I think automation can help eliminate the economic incentive to exploit people. If a machine can do dangerous, repetitive work more cheaply and reliably, there’s less reason to force a person to do it. That’s a powerful opportunity.

But automation doesn’t end slavery by itself. Slavery is also about coercion, vulnerability, and people having no way out. You still need laws that are enforced, accountability in supply chains, and real alternatives for workers. The goal should be to free people from exploitation while giving them a path to a better livelihood.
